question: Predicting time to conversion from MCI to AD in MCI cohorts with survival models, evaluated by C-index on an internal hold-out set. P-344 uses ADNI (902 MCI, 271 in the test set) with 14 final features: APOE e4, FDG-PET, four structural MRI volumes and eight cognitive or functional scores. P-309 uses NACC UDS (3,674 MCI, about 1,102 in the validation set) with 13 predictors: age, BMI, education, MoCA, three CDR domain scores, Craft Story delayed recall, Benson figure copy, two category-fluency scores, companion-reported memory decline and APOE e4 count. The task and population class (MCI in research or memory-clinic cohorts) match. The channel being compared, clinical and cognitive data, is shared, and P-344's multimodal model matches on it. The allowed differences are cohort, imaging features, horizon, sample size and validation split.
metric: C-index (concordance index) with C-index, on the test or validation split in both papers.

figures.P-344: Test set n = 271, stratified on event status, so about 42.0% x 271 = 114 events and 157 censored. RSF 0.878, CoxPH 0.863, Weibull 0.862, CoxEN 0.860, GBSA 0.803. The printed bootstrap 95% CIs are +/-0.001 (RSF 0.877-0.879, CoxPH 0.862-0.864), too narrow to be sampling intervals for 271 subjects, so intervals are derived instead. Hanley-McNeil, applied to the C-index as an approximation, with n1 = 114, n0 = 157. RSF: Q1 = 0.878/1.122 = 0.7825, Q2 = 2(0.878^2)/1.878 = 0.8210, SE = 0.0227, 95% CI 0.833-0.923. CoxPH: SE = 0.0240, CI 0.816-0.910.
figures.P-309: Validation set = 30% of 3,674, about 1,102, of whom about 27% (about 298) developed AD and 804 did not. RSF 0.781, XGBoost 0.781, Cox 0.798 (abstract; the results text gives 0.797 with APOE e4 and 0.798 without). No intervals are printed. Hanley-McNeil, RSF: Q1 = 0.781/1.219 = 0.6407, Q2 = 2(0.781^2)/1.781 = 0.6850, SE = 0.0170, 95% CI 0.748-0.814. Cox 0.798: SE = 0.0166, CI 0.766-0.830.
figures.between_studies: RSF: 0.878 vs 0.781, z = 0.097/sqrt(0.0227^2 + 0.0170^2) = 3.42. Cox: 0.863 vs 0.798, z = 0.065/sqrt(0.0240^2 + 0.0166^2) = 2.23. Each estimate lies outside the other's interval, in both directions and for both model families. Robustness: doubling P-344's SE still leaves P-309's RSF 0.781 below P-344's lower bound (0.789). For Cox, doubling P-344's SE would bring its lower bound to 0.769, below 0.798, but P-309's own interval still excludes 0.863.
figures.within_study_ordering: This is the quantity the ledger disputes. RSF minus Cox is +0.015 in P-344 and -0.017 in P-309. The SE of each difference depends on the correlation between the two models' C-indices on the same test set, which neither paper reports. At r = 0.5: P-344 -0.031 to 0.061, P-309 -0.050 to 0.016, so each estimate lies inside the other's interval. At r = 0.8: -0.014 to 0.044 and -0.038 to 0.004, so each lies just outside. The ordering is not decidable from the texts. P-344's paired Wilcoxon over 1,000 bootstrap replicates is not a test on subjects. Gradient boosting trails Cox in both papers (GBSA 0.803 vs 0.863; XGBoost 0.781 vs 0.798).

matched_figure_check: No matched figure exists. P-344 reports no C-index for a model without imaging: its per-category analysis (Fig. 5) gives only Kaplan-Meier stratification and log-rank tests. P-309 has no imaging predictors (CSF and radiomics were excluded for missingness). P-309 prints time-dependent AUCs at 1-5 years, and P-344 prints none, so no common horizon is reported.
performance_validity: Neither study is excluded under Section 3.5: P-344's best is 0.878 and P-309's 0.798, both below 0.97, with internal validation only in both. P-344 describes missForest imputation and Lasso-Cox feature selection before it states 'After preprocessing, the data was randomly split'. If selection used the full cohort, P-344's test figure would be optimistic. That is a candidate explanation, not an exclusion.

candidate_explanations.difference: Imaging predictors: P-344's final model includes FDG-PET and four MRI volumes; P-309 has none and says CSF and radiomics might add more.
candidate_explanations.quote: (a) gene expression (ApoE_ε4), (b) PET (FDG), (c) MRI (Hippocampus, Entorhinal, Fusiform, MidTemp), (d) cognitive tests (LDELTOTAL, RAVLT_immediate, RAVLT_learning, RAVLT_perc_forgetting, CDRSB, FAQ, ADAS13, TRABSCOR)

candidate_explanations.difference: Imaging predictors were not available to P-309's model; the authors suggest they may have a greater effect.
candidate_explanations.quote: this model was not compared with the results adding these two types of predictors [ 32 ], but these predictors may have a greater eﬀect on the progression of AD

candidate_explanations.difference: Cohort: the ADNI research cohort (ADNIMERGE 2005-2023) against NACC UDS memory-clinic data.
candidate_explanations.quote: In this study, we used the NACC database and combined the predictor selection method with ensemble learning.

candidate_explanations.difference: Follow-up and horizon: follow-up up to 16 years with a median time to progression of 6 years (ADNI), against a median follow-up of 24.5 months (NACC). P-309 reports that its discrimination falls at longer horizons, so the direction of this effect on Harrell's C across cohorts is not established.
candidate_explanations.quote: with extended follow-up data spanning up to 16 years
The median follow-up time was 24.5 months (IQR 13.4–40.4).

candidate_explanations.difference: Event proportion and definition: 42.0% progressed to AD in ADNI, against about 27% diagnosed with AD in NACC (AD diagnosed at the most recent visit).
candidate_explanations.quote: In the validation set, approximately 27 % of the subjects developed AD.

candidate_explanations.difference: Validation and preprocessing: imputation and Lasso feature selection are described before the 70/30 split in P-344, so possible optimism; P-309 uses a 7:3 split with 5-fold CV inside the training set.
candidate_explanations.quote: After preprocessing, the data was randomly split into non-overlapping training (n = 631, 70%) and testing (n = 271, 30%) sets

candidate_explanations.difference: Evaluation-set size: 271 test subjects against about 1,102 validation subjects.
candidate_explanations.quote: The dataset was divided into a training set and a validation set at a 7:3 ra- tio.

reason: Both papers predict time to MCI-to-AD conversion from clinical and cognitive predictors, P-344 adding PET and MRI, and report the C-index on an internal hold-out. P-344's RSF 0.878 and CoxPH 0.863 lie outside the Hanley-McNeil intervals derived for P-309's 0.781 and 0.798 over about 1,102 validation subjects, and the reverse holds too (z = 3.42 and 2.23). No matched figure closes the gap. The ledger's own dispute, the reversal of the RSF-versus-Cox ordering (+0.015 against -0.017), cannot be decided from the texts: it depends on an inter-model correlation neither paper reports, and P-344's +/-0.001 bootstrap intervals are not sampling intervals. The pair therefore qualifies on the absolute level of discrimination, not on the ordering. Imaging predictors, cohort, horizon, event definition, preprocessing before the split and test size are candidate explanations, none shown to be sufficient. The operator's 2026-09-24 grounds (different predictor sets and horizons) are among these explanations; under this rule they are allowed differences and do not block the pair.

quotes.quote: RSF achieved the best performance with a score of 0.878 (95% CI: 0.877–0.879), followed by CoxPH with 0.863 (95% CI: 0.862–0.864)
After preprocessing, the data was randomly split into non-overlapping training (n = 631, 70%) and testing (n = 271, 30%) sets using stratified sampling based on event status
The median time to progression was 6 years (95% CI: 5–7 years)
Among the 61 features, 27 were removed due to missing values exceeding 25% in the MCI subset.
In the validation set, the concordance indices were 0.781 (RSF), 0.781 (XGBoost), and 0.798 (Cox)
A total of 3674 subjects with MCI were included.
In the validation set, approximately 27 % of the subjects developed AD.
the C-index of the Cox model was 0.797, and the Integrated Brier Score was 0.087.
the prediction ability decreases as the prediction time increases.
